hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The alloy is expected to exhibit an improvement in high-temperature yield strength and creep resistance by roughly 10–15% relative to the same alloy processed with a conventional water quench, due to enhanced precipitate refinement.
hypothesis.baseline: Al4.4Co26Cr19Fe18Ni27Ti5.6 alloy processed by standard water quench followed by aging at 750 °C.
hypothesis.boundary: This intervention is applicable when the material processing permits cryogenic quenching without inducing cracking or unwanted residual stresses and is targeted for tests at temperatures between 650 °C and 750 °C.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The degree of further suppression of initial precipitation and the resulting nucleation density during aging is not precisely known; diffusion kinetics during cryogenic quench may vary the extent of improvement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy specimens: one set quenched in water (baseline) and one set quenched in liquid nitrogen immediately after solution annealing. Subject both sets to identical aging treatments (e.g., 750 °C for 10–50 h). Characterize precipitate size/distribution via TEM and APT and perform elevated-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., compression or tensile tests at ~700 °C).
measurements: Precipitate size distribution and volume fraction (TEM, APT)
Elevated-temperature yield strength
Creep resistance under constant load
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cryogenically quenched specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant (≥10%) improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength and/or creep resistance, or if the precipitate dispersion is not measurably finer and more uniform compared to the water-quenched specimens, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C14

source_paper.title: Influence of Ti on the Tensile Properties of the High-Strength Powder Metallurgy High Entropy Alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: the observation in the paper that ethanol wet-milling increases Ti-rich oxide contamination (PMC7040714::web::011, PMC7040714::web::020) and the knowledge that oxygen-induced oxide inclusions detrimentally affect mechanical properties in high-temperature applications.
hypotheses.what_is_new: A process-oriented modification aimed at reducing interstitial oxygen contamination during mechanical alloying to enhance high-temperature mechanical performance, rather than modifying alloy composition or applying post-processing heat treatments.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Optimizing the mechanical alloying route by replacing the ethanol wet-milling step with a dry milling process under ultra-high purity argon combined with an in situ deoxidation step will minimize Ti-rich oxide inclusion formation, enhancing the HEA’s elevated-temperature ductility and fatigue resistance.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A titanium- and nickel-containing HEA produced via powder metallurgy involving mechanical alloying that currently employs an ethanol wet-milling step, resulting in ~3.5% Ti-rich oxide inclusions.
hypothesis.intervention: Eliminate the ethanol wet-milling step by adopting a dry milling process in a strictly controlled ultra-high purity argon atmosphere along with a chemical deoxidation agent (or in situ getter) during milling.
hypothesis.conditions: Mechanical alloying followed by SPS and annealing; testing conducted under elevated temperature (e.g., 600–800 °C) tensile and cyclic (fatigue) loading conditions mimicking extreme applications.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A significantly reduced content of Ti-rich oxide inclusions and a cleaner, more homogeneous FCC matrix microstructure.
hypothesis.mechanism: Oxygen introduced during ethanol wet-milling fosters the formation of Ti-rich oxide particles, which act as stress concentrators under elevated or cyclic loading, reducing ductility and fatigue life. By minimizing the oxygen contamination during milling, fewer deleterious oxide inclusions form, leading to improved ductility and fatigue resistance at elevated temperatures.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Enhanced elevated-temperature ductility and improved fatigue life (potential improvements could be moderate, yet clearly higher than the current state) relative to the HEA produced by ethanol wet-milling, with a potential slight increase in strength due to the reduction of stress concentrators.
hypothesis.baseline: The currently reported HEA produced with ethanol wet-milling that exhibits a measurable level of oxide inclusions (≈3.5%), limiting high-temperature ductility and fatigue performance.
hypothesis.boundary: Applicable to the HEA processing route via powder metallurgy; improvements are expected primarily when the processing oxygen level is a critical limiting factor. Benefits must be validated within the 600–800 °C testing range.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The absolute quantitative improvement in ductility or fatigue resistance is uncertain if residual oxygen sources remain or if the milling process introduces other defects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of HEA powders: one using the original ethanol wet-milling and one using the optimized dry milling in ultra-high purity argon with in situ deoxidation. Process both batches via identical SPS and annealing steps. Assess the oxide inclusion content using microscopic analyses (e.g., SEM/TEM) and perform elevated-temperature tensile and fatigue tests.
measurements: Volume fraction and size distribution of oxide inclusions by microscopy
Elevated-temperature ductility and tensile properties
Fatigue life under cyclic loading at elevated temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the dry-milled samples do not exhibit a significant reduction in oxide inclusion content or do not show measurable improvements in elevated-temperature ductility and fatigue life compared to the wet-milled control, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C4

source_paper.title: The High Temperature Tensile and Creep Behaviors of High Entropy Superalloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: The concept of precipitation strengthening in HEAs as illustrated in the paper (PMC5627260::web::004::results) and background principles of microstructural refinement enhancing mechanical performance (TXT::wikipedia::Solid_solution_strengthening::009).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces an alternative processing route (rapid solidification) to refine the inherent microstructure of a Ti–Ni-based HEA, aiming to achieve a more uniform and optimally sized γ′ precipitate distribution tailored for improved performance at elevated temperatures – a novel approach not explored in the referenced paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Employ rapid solidification (RS) processing to refine and homogenize the distribution of γ′ precipitates in the Ti–Ni HEA, thereby enhancing high-temperature mechanical performance.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A single-phase, Ti–Ni-containing high-entropy alloy produced by conventional vacuum arc melting and directional solidification, exhibiting relatively coarse dendritic structures and a γ/γ′ microstructure with some heterogeneity in precipitate distribution.
hypothesis.intervention: Implement a rapid solidification technique (such as melt spinning or gas atomization followed by consolidation) to dramatically increase cooling rates during alloy solidification, aiming to reduce solute segregation and refine the microstructure. Follow this with a modified heat treatment tailored to the refined starting microstructure.
hypothesis.conditions: Apply RS processing under controlled inert atmosphere to ensure high cooling rates (e.g., >10^5 K/s). Subsequent heat treatments (solution and aging) should be optimized for the refined starting structure. Mechanical testing should be performed at elevated temperatures (750–1000 °C) relevant to creep and tensile applications.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A homogenously refined microstructure featuring a uniform distribution of fine, coherently precipitated L12 γ′ particles with reduced size dispersion and minimized coarse carbides or dendritic segregation.
hypothesis.mechanism: Rapid solidification minimizes segregation and refines grain and precipitate sizes. The resulting uniform and fine γ′ distribution increases the barriers to dislocation motion via enhanced Orowan looping and more effective dislocation pinning. This microstructural refinement is expected to improve both the tensile yield strength and the creep resistance due to a more homogeneous internal stress field during high-temperature deformation (supported by principles of solid solution and precipitation strengthening as discussed in TXT::wikipedia::Solid_solution_strengthening::009).
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: RS-processed HEA samples should demonstrate improved high-temperature tensile strength and lower creep strain rates compared to samples produced by conventional processing, with an expected moderate performance boost (potentially around 10–15% improvement), though the exact magnitude remains to be determined.
hypothesis.baseline: The HEA produced via conventional vacuum arc melting and directional solidification, which exhibits a coarser microstructure with inherent chemical heterogeneities.
hypothesis.boundary: Effective only if the RS processing can be successfully applied to the alloy without introducing detrimental defects such as porosity or amorphous regions, and provided that subsequent heat treatments can develop the desired γ/γ′ microstructure within the refined matrix. It is applicable under high-temperature testing regimes below the γ′ dissolution temperature (~1150 °C).
hypothesis.uncertainty: The extent to which RS processing will improve the distribution and stability of γ′ precipitates, and whether the processing route can be scaled to produce defect-free materials consistently, remains to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one using conventional casting and directional solidification, and one using rapid solidification followed by the optimized heat treatment. Characterize their microstructures via SEM/TEM to assess precipitate size and distribution. Then, perform elevated-temperature tensile and creep tests under identical conditions.
measurements: Grain and precipitate size distribution via SEM/TEM
Homogeneity of the microstructure via EDS mapping
Tensile strength and creep performance at 750–1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the RS-processed samples do not show a significantly refined and more homogeneous precipitate distribution, or if there is no measurable improvement (or a degradation) in high-temperature mechanical properties compared to the conventionally processed samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C7

source_paper.title: Design and Fabrication of New High Entropy Alloys for Evaluating Titanium Replacements in Additive Manufacturing.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s discussion of laser additive manufacturing process optimization, extending it by introducing controlled substrate heating to engineer a graded microstructure tailored for high-temperature performance—a concept not addressed in the paper.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces the novel concept of using a deliberate substrate thermal gradient to produce dual-phase, graded microstructures within a multi-component HEA, combining benefits of both fine and coarse grains for improved high-temperature mechanical properties.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Implementing controlled substrate heating to generate a thermal gradient during laser additive manufacturing of a multi-component Ti–Ni–Al–Cr high-entropy alloy will create a graded grain structure with fine, equiaxed grains near the surface and coarser, aligned grains in the interior, thereby enhancing elevated-temperature fatigue and creep resistance.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A multi-component Ti–Ni–Al–Cr high-entropy alloy produced via laser additive manufacturing, initially exhibiting a homogeneous, single-phase solid-solution microstructure with relatively uniform grain sizes.
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce a programmable substrate heating system that creates a controlled temperature gradient during deposition. This thermal management will be designed to slow cooling in specific zones, enabling a dual-phase microstructure with refined, equiaxed grains on the surfaces (improving resistance to environmental degradation) and columnar, load-bearing grains in the interior (optimizing directional mechanical strength).
hypothesis.conditions: Elevated-temperature testing in the range of 550–750 °C under fatigue and creep loading conditions relevant to aerospace and high-temperature structural applications.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A graded microstructure characterized by a fine-grained surface layer and a coarser, directionally aligned interior structure, along with controlled residual stress profiles across the build.
hypothesis.mechanism: The engineered thermal gradient via substrate heating modulates the cooling rate locally during solidification. A slower cooling rate at the substrate interface promotes grain coarsening and alignment, while a faster cooling at the outer layers produces fine, equiaxed grains. This dual-microstructural approach optimizes load transfer and inhibits premature crack initiation, thereby enhancing high-temperature fatigue and creep resistance.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The graded microstructure alloy is expected to show improved fatigue life (potentially in the range of 10–20% improvement) and enhanced creep resistance compared to the conventionally processed, homogeneous microstructure HEA, though exact improvements are subject to experimental verification.
hypothesis.baseline: The baseline is the HEA produced via standard laser additive manufacturing without any additional substrate heating, resulting in a uniform, single-phase grain structure.
hypothesis.boundary: The intervention applies to multi-component HEAs where substrate temperature can be precisely controlled. Overheating or too shallow a gradient might yield unwanted grain coarsening or residual stress accumulation that could impair performance.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise thermal gradient required to achieve the optimal graded structure is uncertain and may vary with alloy composition; detailed thermal modeling and process iteration are necessary.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of HEA samples: one using the standard laser additive manufacturing process and one using the controlled substrate heating approach to generate a thermal gradient. Characterize the microstructure using EBSD to confirm the graded structure, and perform elevated-temperature fatigue and creep tests over 550–750 °C.
measurements: Grain size and distribution (via EBSD) distinguishing surface vs. interior
Residual stress profile mapping
High-temperature fatigue life and creep rate measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with controlled substrate heating do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in fatigue life and creep resistance (e.g., less than 10% improvement) compared to the baseline, or if the expected graded microstructure is not achieved, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C1

source_paper.title: Manufacturing of Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti High-Entropy Alloy Using Directed Energy Deposition and Evaluation of Its Microstructure, Tensile Strength, and Microhardness.

hypotheses.builds_on: The observed coarse-grain microstructure in the DED-produced HEA (PMC11396108::web::014) and general principles of grain boundary strengthening from materials science teaching texts.
hypotheses.what_is_new: Rather than focusing on precipitation strengthening, this hypothesis explores a microstructural modification pathway—grain refinement via SPD—to improve high-temperature mechanical properties in the primary Ti-Ni containing HEA.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Severe plastic deformation (SPD) post-processing, such as high-pressure torsion, can refine the grain size of the Ti- and Ni-based single-phase HEA, improving its elevated-temperature mechanical properties through grain boundary strengthening.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A single-phase, coarse-grained Ti- and Ni-containing high-entropy alloy produced by directed energy deposition.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a severe plastic deformation technique (e.g., high-pressure torsion or friction stir processing) at a controlled elevated temperature to refine the grain structure.
hypothesis.conditions: Processing at a temperature low enough to avoid unwanted phase changes (e.g., below 600 °C) but high enough to facilitate plastic deformation, with an applied strain sufficient to reduce grain size to the sub-micron or fine micron scale; testing under elevated-temperature conditions up to ~700 °C.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Grain refinement, leading to increased grain boundary area which reinforces the material via the Hall–Petch effect.
hypothesis.mechanism: Refined grains enhance yield strength by impeding dislocation motion at grain boundaries; in high-temperature environments, finer grain structures can also help improve creep resistance up to a point. However, the trade-off with grain-boundary sliding must be carefully managed, which is why a moderate SPD process is targeted.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: A measurable increase in elevated-temperature yield strength and improved microhardness due to the refined grain structure; the degree of strengthening is expected to be in line with classical Hall–Petch predictions, though exact values depend on the attained grain size.
hypothesis.baseline: The original coarse-grained single-phase HEA produced by DED, which exhibited relatively lower yield strength and microhardness at high temperatures.
hypothesis.boundary: Effective primarily for temperatures where grain boundary strengthening is active (likely below 700 °C) and where the SPD process does not induce harmful phase transformations. Extreme grain boundary sliding at very high temperatures may counteract benefits.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The long-term thermal stability of the refined grain structure under prolonged high-temperature exposure is uncertain, and excessive grain boundary area could lead to accelerated grain boundary creep if not optimized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of HEA samples: one set processed by SPD (e.g., high-pressure torsion) and one control set retaining the as-DED microstructure. Evaluate both sets with microstructural characterization (SEM/EBSD for grain size) and perform high-temperature tensile and creep tests.
measurements: Grain size distribution via EBSD
Yield strength and ductility at elevated temperatures
Creep behavior under constant load at temperatures around 600–700 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SPD-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant grain size reduction and corresponding improvements in mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength and creep resistance) over the control samples, or if deleterious effects (e.g., premature grain-boundary failure) are observed, the hypothesis is falsified.

expert_context.question: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

hypotheses.label: C3

source_paper.title: The Microstructures, Mechanical Properties, and Deformation Mechanism of B2-Hardened NbTiAlZr-Based Refractory High-Entropy Alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: While the paper identifies that dynamic recrystallization and dislocation annihilation contribute to strain softening, this hypothesis introduces carbide precipitation as a means to impede these processes, leveraging metallurgical principles known from carbon-alloyed systems.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It suggests a novel microalloying strategy—adding a trace of carbon to enable in situ formation of nano-carbides—to improve high-temperature mechanical performance in a Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy, an intervention not previously reported in the study.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Microalloying with a trace amount of carbon (0.5–1 at%) will promote the in situ formation of fine TiC (and/or related Ni–Ti carbide) nanoparticles that impede dislocation motion and grain boundary migration, thus enhancing the elevated-temperature yield strength of a Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A conventionally cast Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy with a B2-ordered structure and a dendritic microstructure established by vacuum melting.
hypothesis.intervention: During the melting process, introduce a controlled carbon addition of 0.5–1 at% so that upon solidification and subsequent low-temperature annealing, dispersed, nano-scale TiC particles form preferentially at dislocation tangles and grain boundaries.
hypothesis.conditions: High-temperature compressive testing in the 1023–1123 K range.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A refined microstructure featuring nano-scale, stable carbide particles distributed within the matrix and along grain boundaries, acting as pinning sites for dislocations and restraining dynamic recrystallization.
hypothesis.mechanism: The in situ formed TiC particles, due to their high thermal stability, provide a barrier to dislocation motion by forcing dislocations to bow or bypass the particles (Orowan looping). In addition, their presence along grain boundaries helps to stabilize the microstructure by limiting GB sliding and migration during high-temperature deformation.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: An improvement in yield strength of roughly 10–15% at high temperatures compared to the untreated alloy, along with a reduced rate of strain softening during deformation.
hypothesis.baseline: The baseline is the Ti–Ni primary HEA without carbon addition, exhibiting the microstructural evolution and yield behavior documented in the paper.
hypothesis.boundary: The carbon content must be controlled between 0.5 and 1 at% to ensure the formation of fine, discrete carbides without triggering a continuous carbide network that could embrittle the alloy; the processing and heat treatment temperatures must be compatible with carbide stability.
hypothesis.uncertainty: Thermodynamic predictions for carbide formation in a multi-principal element system are challenging, so the precise morphology and volume fraction of carbides formed are uncertain until experimentally validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two alloy batches: one standard Ti–Ni primary HEA and one with the 0.5–1 at% carbon addition. After identical casting and a controlled post-cast annealing treatment, perform high-temperature (1023–1123 K) compression tests and use TEM/EBSD to verify the formation, distribution, and morphology of TiC nanoparticles.
measurements: Yield strength and corresponding high-temperature stress–strain curves
Microstructural characterization to quantify carbide size, distribution, and volume fraction via TEM/EDS
Fractography to ensure ductility is not adversely affected
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-added alloy does not exhibit at least a 10% improvement in yield strength and microstructural analysis fails to confirm a fine, well-distributed population of TiC nanoparticles compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C4

source_paper.title: High-content ductile coherent nanoprecipitates achieve ultrastrong high-entropy alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: the principle from PMC6170471 that a refined, homogeneous precursor state can enhance spinodal decomposition to yield coherent nanoprecipitates; here extended by using rapid solidification to pre-refine the microstructure in a Ti–Ni primary HEA.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces rapid solidification as a novel processing route for Ti–Ni primary HEAs to pre-establish an ultrafine, homogeneous microstructure that tailors the subsequent spinodal decomposition kinetics and promotes a superior distribution of strengthening nanoprecipitates.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Utilizing rapid solidification processing to produce an ultrafine-grained Ti–Ni primary HEA precursor will create a more homogeneous and refined supersaturated state, thereby enhancing spinodal decomposition kinetics during aging and resulting in a finer, more uniformly dispersed population of coherent nanoprecipitates at elevated temperatures.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy consisting primarily of titanium and nickel along with at least three additional elements in near-equiatomic proportions, initially prepared via conventional casting to yield a coarse-grained, homogeneous single-phase structure.
hypothesis.intervention: Employ rapid solidification methods (e.g., melt spinning or gas atomization) during alloy fabrication to dramatically increase the cooling rate, yielding an ultrafine-grained structure with suppressed elemental segregation and enhanced supersaturation.
hypothesis.conditions: The rapid solidification process must yield an ultrafine microstructure without altering the overall composition (elements remain within 5–35 at%). Subsequent thermo-mechanical processing (solution treatment, cold working, and aging at ~600 °C for 1 hour) will then be applied to activate spinodal decomposition.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: An ultrafine-grained matrix that, after standard thermomechanical processing, develops a high density of coherent nanoprecipitates (e.g., Ni3Al-type L12 phases or analogous ordering) uniformly distributed throughout the near-equiatomic matrix.
hypothesis.mechanism: Rapid solidification introduces a very fine grain structure and a high degree of supersaturation by quenching in a more homogeneous state. This refined precursor state accelerates the nucleation of spinodal decomposition during subsequent aging, resulting in a significantly refined and uniform dispersion of coherent nanoprecipitates. These nanoprecipitates, with their low lattice misfit and diffuse interfaces, more effectively obstruct dislocation motion at elevated temperatures.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to a conventionally cast alloy, the rapid-solidified and aged alloy is expected to exhibit improved elevated-temperature yield and ultimate tensile strengths – potentially a 15–25% increase – with a finer precipitate size (e.g., reduced by 20–30%) and enhanced uniformity.
hypothesis.baseline: A Ti–Ni primary HEA processed from conventionally cast precursor material and subjected to the same solution treatment, cold rolling, and aging at ~600 °C for 1 hour.
hypothesis.boundary: The rapid solidification processing parameters must be optimized to avoid amorphization or undesirable phases; the final composition and processing route must remain within the HEA definitions.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While rapid solidification has been broadly shown to refine microstructures in alloys, the exact degree to which it enhances spinodal decomposition in a Ti–Ni primary HEA is moderately uncertain and may depend on processing nuances.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the Ti–Ni primary HEA: one via conventional casting and one via rapid solidification (using melt spinning or gas atomization). Subject both to identical solution treatment, cold rolling, and aging at 600 °C for 1 hour. Characterize grain size and precipitate distribution using TEM/EBSD and perform elevated-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: Grain size distribution (via EBSD)
Size, volume fraction, and dispersion uniformity of coherent nanoprecipitates (via TEM/APT)
Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility at high temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapid-solidified alloy does not show a statistically significant refinement in grain size and precipitate morphology, with a corresponding improvement (at least 10–15% increase) in high-temperature mechanical properties compared to the conventional alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C9

source_paper.title: The Effect of Al and Ti Additions on Solid Solution Strengthening and Precipitation Hardening in CoNiFe Medium-Entropy Alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: the concept from the paper that precipitation strengthening is a potent mechanism in HEAs, extended by integrating grain refinement via rapid solidification to further enhance high-temperature mechanical properties.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It introduces a processing route change—rapid solidification—to create an ultrafine-grained HEA that, upon subsequent aging, achieves a synergistic strengthening effect combining grain boundary and precipitation hardening, a strategy not addressed in the original study.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Adopt a rapid solidification processing route (e.g., melt spinning) in a Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy to achieve an ultrafine-grained microstructure that, upon a subsequent controlled aging treatment, results in a high density of fine, uniformly distributed precipitates, thereby enhancing elevated-temperature mechanical properties.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a composition around Ti 40, Ni 40, Co 7, Cr 6, and Al 7 (all within the 5–35 at% range) produced by conventional casting and homogenization, exhibiting a coarse grain structure with a standard precipitation response.
hypothesis.intervention: Employ rapid solidification (melt spinning) during alloy production to drastically refine the grain size. Follow this with a standard homogenization heat treatment and an optimized aging treatment (e.g., 750°C for 3 hours) designed to nucleate and grow fine precipitates.
hypothesis.conditions: All elements must adhere to the compositional HEA limits. The rapid solidification process must be optimized (e.g., high cooling rates on the order of 10^5 K/s) to achieve ultrafine grains without compromising alloy homogeneity. Elevated-temperature mechanical tests are conducted from 600 to 800°C.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: An ultrafine-grained matrix with a high density of grain boundaries which, together with a refined distribution of nanoscale precipitates (similar to Ni3Ti or related phases), promotes enhanced dislocation hindrance and grain boundary strengthening.
hypothesis.mechanism: Rapid solidification significantly refines the grain size by suppressing dendritic growth and allows for a higher nucleation rate. The subsequent aging treatment leverages the high number of grain boundaries, which serve as additional nucleation sites for precipitates. This synergistic microstructure (grain refinement plus fine precipitation) enhances strength via both Hall–Petch and precipitation hardening mechanisms, crucial for elevated-temperature performance.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: An enhancement of yield strength and creep resistance by approximately 15–30% at high temperatures (600–800°C) compared to the conventionally cast and homogenized alloy.
hypothesis.baseline: The same HEA composition produced by conventional casting and homogenization, followed by the standard aging treatment, resulting in a relatively coarse grain structure and less refined precipitate distribution.
hypothesis.boundary: The rapid solidification processing must be capable of achieving ultrafine grains without causing compositional segregation. The aging treatment should be optimized to prevent excessive grain growth while promoting nanoscale precipitate formation.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While the beneficial effects of grain refinement and fine precipitation are well established, the precise balance of processing parameters to achieve the desired microstructure in a complex HEA is not fully predictable, making the exact magnitude of improvement somewhat uncertain.

Use microprobe or atom probe tomography to verify the oxygen content and distribution. Then, conduct elevated-temperature mechanical tests (such as yield testing and creep tests at 650–750 °C).
measurements: Oxygen content and distribution analysis (e.g., via APT or microprobe)
Elevated-temperature yield strength
Creep rate at the designated test temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant enhancement in yield strength (e.g., improvement less than 5% beyond experimental scatter) or if deleterious oxide formation is detected that undermines mechanical integrity, the hypothesis is falsified.
